Week 3 Demo Cue Sheet

Every slide in both Week 3 decks, with the commands that show it working. One command per line. Each line has a copy button, a short explanation, and the output you should get. Deck A uses turtlesim — one small program that has a topic, a service, an action and parameters, so the whole lecture runs against one window. The last part uses TurtleBot 3 in Gazebo. Deck B uses the two packages you build this week.

How to use this page

  1. Each command is on its own line. Press Copy, paste it into your terminal, press Enter. Then read the next line. Never copy two lines at once.
  2. The $ is not part of the command. It is the prompt your terminal prints. The copy button leaves it out for you.
  3. Check your output. Under most commands there is a green box that shows what the screen should say. If your screen is different, stop and fix it before the next line.
  4. Some commands are meant to fail. They have a red box instead of a green one. The error is the lesson.
  5. The photos are real. They come from the same computer that made the slides, so your screen should look very close to them.

Before you type anything

Six words you need

Every command below uses these words. If one of them is unclear, the command that uses it will also be unclear.

nodeOne running program. turtlesim_node is a node. Your Python file becomes a node when you run it.
topicA named channel for a stream of data. One node sends, any number of nodes listen. Nobody replies.
serviceA question and one answer. You ask, you wait a short time, you get a reply. Like a phone call.
actionA long job. You send a goal, you get progress updates while it runs, then a final result.
parameterA setting inside a running node. You can read it and change it from outside, without restarting the node.
packageA folder of code that ROS 2 can find and run. You build packages with colcon; they live in a workspace.

Before the lecture starts

Four terminals

Open these four windows before the room fills. The reason is simple: nothing should be restarted in the middle of the demo. If a node stops, everything connected to it stops too, and you lose your place.

T1

turtlesim

Start it once. Leave it open for Parts 1 to 6. Keep the window next to the slides — Parts 4 and 6 are shown in this window, not in a terminal.

T2

Your commands

You type almost everything here. Make the font two sizes bigger than normal, or the back row cannot read it.

T3

Gazebo · TurtleBot 3

Part 7 only. Start it during Part 6. It needs 20 to 30 seconds to open, and waiting in silence is worse than starting early.

T4

Your own nodes

Deck B only. This is where wheel_publisher, odom_node and driver run.

Start turtlesim

  1. $ros2 run turtlesim turtlesim_node

    T1 What it does: starts the turtle program. A blue window opens with one turtle in the middle. Leave this running.

Go back to the starting state

Run these four lines any time the demo gets messy — for example after you add a second turtle or change the background colour. They put turtlesim back to how it looked at the start.

  1. $ros2 service call /reset std_srvs/srv/Empty '{}'

    What it does: clears the drawing and moves the turtle back to the middle.

  2. $ros2 service call /kill turtlesim/srv/Kill "{name: 'scout'}"

    What it does: removes the second turtle called scout. Only needed if you already ran the spawn demo on slide 20.

  3. $ros2 param set /turtlesim background_r 69

    What it does: sets the red part of the background back to 69.

  4. $ros2 param set /turtlesim background_g 86

    What it does: sets the green part back to 86.

  5. $ros2 param set /turtlesim background_b 255

    What it does: sets the blue part back to 255. Together, 69 / 86 / 255 is turtlesim's normal blue.

    You will see
    Set parameter successful

Run these once before the lecture too. Then the colour change in Part 6 is clearly a change, and not just the colour it always was.

Three things that break the demo

A clean Ubuntu 24.04 machine has none of these problems. All three exist on the teaching laptop. Each one fails in a way that does not tell you the real reason.

1

Anaconda breaks colcon build. If Anaconda is active, CMake uses the Anaconda Python instead of the system Python. That Python does not have the empy module, so building an interface package stops with No module named 'em'.

Fix: run conda deactivate. If the error stays, also run unset CONDA_PREFIX. This problem starts in Week 3, because Week 3 is the first week with a CMake package.

2

Snap paths kill every window. A terminal opened from a snap application carries library paths that point into /snap/core20. turtlesim and Gazebo then stop immediately with undefined symbol: __libc_pthread_init.

Fix: run source shared/screenshots/rosenv.sh. It removes those paths. The screenshot script uses the same file, so the demo and the pictures in the slides run in the same environment.

3

Other people's nodes appear in your list. On a shared network, ROS 2 connects to every computer using the same domain number. Then ros2 topic list shows thirty topics you never started.

Fix: run export ROS_DOMAIN_ID=77 before the lecture, and ask the class to do the same. This also removes the "duplicate node name" warning.

Deck A — Communication Models

EE414_W03A_communication_models.pdf · 35 slides

The idea of this lecture is simple: one ordinary node already uses all four ways of talking. Slide 7 proves it. One command prints four headings, and Parts 3 to 6 are those four headings, one at a time.

PART 1

Interaction Models

4Talk

Selecting an Interaction Model

Ask the class to sort three jobs before you show the answer: send the laser readings, ask how much battery is left, drive to the far corner. Do not give the answer yet. Slide 7 gives it for you.

5Talk

Three Ways to Choose Wrongly

The table is the whole slide. Say clearly that every row is a mistake they will make in their Week 11 project, because they will.

6Live

Turtlesim: One Node, All Four Mechanisms

Start the turtle moving first. The window should be doing something before you explain what is inside it.

  1. $ros2 topic pub -r 10 /turtle1/cmd_vel geometry_msgs/msg/Twist '{linear: {x: 2.0}, angular: {z: 1.8}}'

    T2 What it does: sends a speed command 10 times per second. linear.x is forward speed. angular.z is turning speed. Forward and turning at the same time draws a circle.

  2. After a few seconds: press Ctrl-C to stop sending. The turtle stops moving straight away.

Notice

Nobody told the turtle to stop. It stopped because the messages stopped. A topic has no memory and no promise — when the sending stops, the behaviour stops.

7Live

Node Introspection: ros2 node info

This is the most important command in the lecture. One command, four headings, and the rest of the deck follows those headings in order.

  1. $ros2 node info /turtlesim

    Expected output — 30 lines
    /turtlesim
  Subscribers:
    /parameter_events: rcl_interfaces/msg/ParameterEvent
    /turtle1/cmd_vel: geometry_msgs/msg/Twist
  Publishers:
    /parameter_events: rcl_interfaces/msg/ParameterEvent
    /rosout: rcl_interfaces/msg/Log
    /turtle1/color_sensor: turtlesim/msg/Color
    /turtle1/pose: turtlesim/msg/Pose
  Service Servers:
    /clear: std_srvs/srv/Empty

    /turtle1/teleport_absolute: turtlesim/srv/TeleportAbsolute
    /turtle1/teleport_relative: turtlesim/srv/TeleportRelative
    /turtlesim/describe_parameters: rcl_interfaces/srv/DescribeParameters

Point at

Four headings: Subscribers and Publishers are topics (Part 3). Service Servers is Part 4. Action Servers is Part 5. The seven services with parameters in the name are Part 6. One small program uses every mechanism in the course.

Now ask the same node four narrower questions. Each verb has the same shape, and each one opens a later part of the lecture.

PART 2

Interface Definitions

9Live

Message Definition Syntax

First show the shape of a message. Then show that same shape filled with zeros. The second command is the one students remember, because it gives them text they can paste.

  1. $ros2 interface show geometry_msgs/msg/Twist

    T2 What it does: prints the fields of the Twist message. Twist is the message every ROS 2 robot uses for speed commands.

    You will see
    # This expresses velocity in free space broken into its linear and angular parts.

Vector3  linear
	float64 x
	float64 y
	float64 z
Vector3  angular
	float64 x
	float64 y
	float64 z
  2. $ros2 interface proto geometry_msgs/msg/Twist

    What it does: prints the same message as an empty example, ready to fill in. Copy it into the ros2 topic pub command from slide 6 and change one number.

    You will see
    "linear:
  x: 0.0
  y: 0.0
  z: 0.0
angular:
  x: 0.0
  y: 0.0
  z: 0.0
"
Notice

Two fields become six numbers. Vector3 is itself a message, so show opens it and prints what is inside. Messages are built from smaller messages.

10Live

Standard Message Definition: LaserScan

  1. $ros2 interface show sensor_msgs/msg/LaserScan

    T2 What it does: prints the message a laser scanner sends. This is the message you will use in Week 6 and Week 11.

    Expected output — the ten fields, with comments
    # Single scan from a planar laser range-finder

std_msgs/Header header       # timestamp and frame of the first ray
	builtin_interfaces/Time stamp
		int32 sec
		uint32 nanosec
	string frame_id

float32 angle_min            # start angle of the scan [rad]
float32 angle_max            # end angle of the scan [rad]
float32 angle_increment      # angular distance between measurements [rad]

float32 time_increment       # time between measurements [seconds]
float32 scan_time            # time between scans [seconds]

float32 range_min            # minimum range value [m]
float32 range_max            # maximum range value [m]

float32[] ranges             # range data [m]
float32[] intensities        # intensity data [device-specific units]
Count them

Ten fields, not seven. The three people always forget are time_increment, scan_time and intensities. An earlier version of this slide was written from memory and had seven. Running the command is what found the mistake.

11Live

The Role of the Message Header

  1. $ros2 interface show std_msgs/msg/Header

    T2 What it does: prints the small message that sits at the top of almost every sensor message.

    You will see
    # Standard metadata for higher-level stamped data types.

# Two-integer timestamp that is expressed as seconds and nanoseconds.
builtin_interfaces/Time stamp
	int32 sec
	uint32 nanosec

# Transform frame with which this data is associated.
string frame_id
  2. $ros2 topic echo /scan --once --field header

    T2 What it does: prints the header of one real laser message. --once means one message then stop. --field header means print only that part. Gazebo must be running (T3) for this line.

    You will see
    stamp:
  sec: 43
  nanosec: 0
frame_id: base_scan
---
Notice

Two questions, two fields. When was this measured — stamp. Measured from where — frame_id. Week 7 is entirely about the second question.

12Live

Count the Separators: Service versus Action

Run these two one after the other and ask the class to count the --- lines. This is the fastest way to teach the difference.

  1. $ros2 interface show turtlesim/srv/Spawn

    T2 What it does: prints a service definition. srv in the name means service.

    You will see — one separator
    float32 x
float32 y
float32 theta
string name # Optional.  A unique name will be created and returned if this is empty
---
string name
  2. $ros2 interface show turtlesim/action/RotateAbsolute

    What it does: prints an action definition. action in the name means action.

    You will see — two separators
    # The desired heading in radians
float32 theta
---
# The angular displacement in radians to the starting position
float32 delta
---
# The remaining rotation in radians
float32 remaining
The rule

One --- is a service: request, then response. Two --- is an action: goal, then result, then feedback. You can tell which mechanism you are looking at before you read a single field name.

13Talk

Custom Definitions: When to Write One, and Where It Lives

This slide points forward to Session B. Give them one test: if a standard message already holds your fields, use it. Most custom messages written in this course are just PoseStamped with different names.

PART 3

Topics

15Live

Definition: Topic

Start the command, then read the definition on the slide while it scrolls. The scrolling behind you is the argument.

  1. $ros2 topic echo /turtle1/pose

    T2 What it does: prints every message the turtle sends about its own position. It never stops. Leave it running while you talk, then press Ctrl-C.

    You will see, again and again
    x: 5.544444561004639
y: 5.544444561004639
theta: 0.0
linear_velocity: 0.0
angular_velocity: 0.0
---
Ask

Did turtlesim change what it does when you connected? No. Was it even told you were there? No. That is what anonymous means. It is also why a topic can never tell you that your listener crashed.

16Live

Topic Inspection, and What It Does Not Tell You

  1. $ros2 topic echo /turtle1/pose --once

    T2 What it does: prints one message and exits. Use this instead of Ctrl-C when you only need to see the shape.

  2. $ros2 topic info /turtle1/cmd_vel

    What it does: prints the message type of a channel, and how many nodes are connected to each end.

    You will see — nothing is publishing
    Type: geometry_msgs/msg/Twist
Publisher count: 0
Subscription count: 1
  3. $ros2 topic pub -r 10 /turtle1/cmd_vel geometry_msgs/msg/Twist '{linear: {x: 2.0}, angular: {z: 1.8}}'

    What it does: starts sending again, in a second terminal, so you can compare the counts. Leave it running for the next line.

  4. $ros2 topic info /turtle1/cmd_vel

    What it does: the same question again, while data is flowing. Then press Ctrl-C on the publisher and run it a third time — the count goes back to 0.

    You will see — while publishing
    Type: geometry_msgs/msg/Twist
Publisher count: 1
Subscription count: 1
The catch

The count is the number of connections, not the amount of data. A publisher that is connected but silent still counts as 1. To ask "is data really arriving?" you need ros2 topic hz, which is on slide 33.

If you have a spare minute: rqt_graph draws the same information as a picture. Show it once. Students who rely on it stop learning the command line.

Services

18Live

Definition: Service

  1. $ros2 service list -t | grep -v parameter

    T2 What it does: lists the services turtlesim offers, with their types.

    You will see — 8 lines
    /clear [std_srvs/srv/Empty]
/kill [turtlesim/srv/Kill]
/reset [std_srvs/srv/Empty]
/spawn [turtlesim/srv/Spawn]
/turtle1/set_pen [turtlesim/srv/SetPen]
/turtle1/teleport_absolute [turtlesim/srv/TeleportAbsolute]
/turtle1/teleport_relative [turtlesim/srv/TeleportRelative]
/turtlesim/get_type_description [type_description_interfaces/srv/GetTypeDescription]
  2. $ros2 service type /spawn

    What it does: asks for the type of one service on its own. You need this type to call the service on slide 20.

    You will see
    turtlesim/srv/Spawn
  3. $ros2 service list -t

    What it does: the same list without the filter. Six more services appear, all with parameters in the name. Point at them and say: that is Part 6, arriving early.

19Talk

Asynchronous Service Clients

A code slide. State the rule and move on. They will not believe it until Session B, when their own client freezes. Promise them that failure now — it makes the Session B demo work.

The rule: use call_async, then add_done_callback. Never wait for a reply inside a callback.

20Live

A Service from the Terminal: Find It, Then Call It

Two steps, and the second one is built from what the first one printed. Read the type off the screen instead of remembering it. That is the real workflow.

  1. $ros2 service list -t | grep -v parameter

    T2 What it does: finds the name /spawn and its type turtlesim/srv/Spawn.

  2. $ros2 service call /spawn turtlesim/srv/Spawn '{x: 2.0, y: 8.0, theta: 0.0, name: "scout"}'

    What it does: asks turtlesim to add a second turtle. The three parts are: the name of the service, its type, and the request in curly brackets. x and y are the position, theta the heading.

    You will see
    waiting for service to become available...
requester: making request: turtlesim.srv.Spawn_Request(x=2.0, y=8.0, theta=0.0, name='scout')

response:
turtlesim.srv.Spawn_Response(name='scout')
Notice

An answer came back. The word response is the whole point of this slide. A topic can never do this.

21Live

Observed Effect of a Service Call

Point at the turtlesim window, not at the terminal. There is a second turtle at position (2, 8), and it was not there ten seconds ago.

  1. $ros2 service call /kill turtlesim/srv/Kill "{name: 'scout'}"

    T2 What it does: removes the second turtle again.

    You will see
    requester: making request: turtlesim.srv.Kill_Request(name='scout')

response:
turtlesim.srv.Kill_Response()
Do not skip

If scout stays alive, every service list for the rest of the lecture is twice as long, and the screenshots on the slides no longer match your screen.

PART 5

Actions

23Live

Definition: Action

  1. $ros2 action list -t

    T2 What it does: lists the actions and their types. turtlesim has exactly one.

    You will see
    /turtle1/rotate_absolute [turtlesim/action/RotateAbsolute]
  2. $ros2 action info /turtle1/rotate_absolute

    What it does: shows which nodes offer this action and which nodes are using it.

    You will see
    Action: /turtle1/rotate_absolute
Action clients: 0
Action servers: 1
    /turtlesim
Ask

Why is rotating an action, but adding a turtle only a service? Because rotating takes time you can watch. Anything you might want to follow, or cancel, is an action.

24Live

The Action Protocol

  1. $ros2 interface show turtlesim/action/RotateAbsolute

    T2 What it does: prints the three parts of the action.

    You will see
    # The desired heading in radians
float32 theta
---
# The angular displacement in radians to the starting position
float32 delta
---
# The remaining rotation in radians
float32 remaining
Three parts

Goal: theta, the heading you want. Result: delta, how far it actually turned. Feedback: remaining, how much is left. Say the word remaining out loud now, so the class recognises it on the next slide.

25Live

Action Feedback During Execution

  1. $ros2 action send_goal /turtle1/rotate_absolute turtlesim/action/RotateAbsolute '{theta: 0.12}' --feedback

    T2 What it does: asks the turtle to turn to heading 0.12 radians. --feedback means "show me the progress while it runs". Without that word you only see the final result.

    Expected output — goal, feedback, result
    Waiting for an action server to become available...
Sending goal:
     theta: 0.12

Feedback:
    remaining: 0.11999999731779099

Goal accepted with ID: 1ee9a293827b43e49e9fcfcb99bff431

Feedback:
    remaining: 0.10399999469518661

Feedback:
    remaining: 0.08799999952316284

    ... six more Feedback blocks, each smaller ...

Result:
    delta: -0.1120000034570694

Goal finished with status: SUCCEEDED
  2. $ros2 action send_goal /turtle1/rotate_absolute turtlesim/action/RotateAbsolute '{theta: 0.0}'

    What it does: the same job with no --feedback. You get the goal, then silence, then the result. The difference between these two runs is the whole reason actions exist.

Keep theta small

Feedback is sent on a timer, so a half turn prints hundreds of lines and pushes the Goal accepted line off the screen. 0.12 gives about eight feedback blocks, which fits.

PART 6

Parameters

27Live

Definition: Parameter

  1. $ros2 param list /turtlesim

    T2 What it does: lists every setting inside the running node.

    You will see — 10 lines
      background_b
  background_g
  background_r
  holonomic
  qos_overrides./parameter_events.publisher.depth
  qos_overrides./parameter_events.publisher.durability
  qos_overrides./parameter_events.publisher.history
  qos_overrides./parameter_events.publisher.reliability
  start_type_description_service
  use_sim_time
Notice

Ten settings. The first three — background_r, _g, _b — are the ones you change on the next slide. The qos_overrides entries belong to ROS 2 itself. One sentence is enough: parameters are not only the ones you write.

28Talk

Declaring Parameters

A code slide. Two lines matter: declare_parameter with a default value, and get_parameter(...).value at the moment you use it. If the value is read once in __init__ and stored, the live change on slide 29 does nothing.

  1. $ros2 param describe /turtlesim background_r

    T2 What it does: shows what the node said when it declared this parameter — its type, its description, and its allowed range. Optional, but it makes the code slide concrete.

    You will see
    Parameter name: background_r
  Type: integer
  Description: Red channel of the background color
  Constraints:
    Min value: 0
    Max value: 255
    Step: 1
29Live

Parameters at Runtime: Read One, Then Change It

  1. $ros2 param get /turtlesim background_r

    T2 What it does: reads one setting out of the running node.

    You will see
    Integer value is: 69
  2. $ros2 param set /turtlesim background_r 200

    What it does: changes the red channel to 200. Watch the T1 window as you press Enter.

    You will see
    Set parameter successful
  3. $ros2 param set /turtlesim background_g 60

    What it does: lowers the green channel to 60.

  4. $ros2 param set /turtlesim background_b 60

    What it does: lowers the blue channel to 60. The window is now red.

30Live

Observed Effect of a Parameter Change

Look at T1. The window is red. Nothing was restarted. That is the whole slide.

Say this

"In Week 5 this number is a controller gain. In Week 11 it is the size of a safety area. You will tune both in exactly this way, with the robot still running."

Put the colour back before Part 7, so the screenshots on the later slides match your screen: background_r 69, background_g 86, background_b 255. The four lines are in Set-up.

PART 7

Application to a Mobile Robot

32Live

The Same Mechanisms on a Mobile Robot

Everything so far was a 2-D turtle. This is the slide where a student decides whether the lecture was about a toy. Start Gazebo during Part 6 so it is already open.

  1. $export TURTLEBOT3_MODEL=burger

    T3 What it does: tells the TurtleBot 3 packages which robot model to load. burger is the small one with a laser scanner.

  2. $ros2 launch turtlebot3_gazebo turtlebot3_world.launch.py

    What it does: starts the simulator with a robot in a small world. A launch file starts many nodes at once. Wait 20 to 30 seconds.

  3. $ros2 topic list

    T2 What it does: the same command as slide 7, on a different robot. The list is longer, but the command did not change.

    You will see — 11 lines
    /clock
/cmd_vel
/imu
/joint_states
/odom
/parameter_events
/robot_description
/rosout
/scan
/tf
/tf_static
  4. $ros2 topic echo /scan --once --field range_max

    What it does: prints how far this laser can see, in metres.

    You will see
    3.5
---
  5. $ros2 topic echo /odom --once --field pose.pose.position

    What it does: prints where the robot thinks it is. The dots mean "go inside this field, then inside that one".

    You will see — near zero, it has not moved
    x: 9.600784784633243e-09
y: -2.2140387636170184e-21
z: 0.0
---
The point

/scan and /odom are topics for the same reason /turtle1/pose was: continuous data, and nobody is waiting for a reply. The mechanism did not change when the robot became real.

If the class is following well: run ros2 run turtlebot3_teleop teleop_keyboard and let a student drive while /odom is echoing on screen.

33Live

What a Topic Costs, and What It Promises

  1. $ros2 topic hz /scan

    T2 What it does: measures how many messages arrive per second. This is the command that answers "is data really arriving?". Press Ctrl-C after about 8 seconds.

    You will see
    average rate: 5.003
	min: 0.196s max: 0.204s std dev: 0.00269s window: 7
average rate: 5.002
	min: 0.195s max: 0.204s std dev: 0.00294s window: 13
average rate: 5.002
	min: 0.194s max: 0.204s std dev: 0.00290s window: 19
  2. $ros2 topic info /scan --verbose

    What it does: prints the delivery rules of the channel — the QoS, or quality of service. These are the promises the connection makes.

    Expected output — the QoS block
    Type: sensor_msgs/msg/LaserScan

Publisher count: 1

Node name: ros_gz_bridge
Node namespace: /
Topic type: sensor_msgs/msg/LaserScan
Endpoint type: PUBLISHER
QoS profile:
  Reliability: RELIABLE
  History (Depth): UNKNOWN
  Durability: VOLATILE
  Lifespan: Infinite
  Deadline: Infinite
  Liveliness: AUTOMATIC
  Liveliness lease duration: Infinite

Subscription count: 0
Read three lines

Reliability: RELIABLE — lost messages are sent again. Durability: VOLATILE — a node that connects late gets nothing that was sent before it arrived. 5 messages per second is what this laser costs you. Those three facts are the whole slide.

Do not add a typed QoS table to this slide. The screenshot already prints all three values, and a table beside it would only repeat the picture.

34Talk

Comparison of the Four Mechanisms

The summary table. Go back one part at a time and name the command that produced each row. The class has now watched all four run against the same node.

Optional close: rqt_graph with turtlesim and the TurtleBot both running. Two robots, one graph, the same four mechanisms.

35Talk

Session B Outline and Deliverables

Tell them to arrive with their Week 2 workspace already building. Session B runs ros2 pkg create at minute three and does not stop after that.

Deck B — Your Own Packages and Interfaces

EE414_W03B_packages_and_interfaces.pdf · 33 slides

This session is a walkthrough. The class types along with you and everyone stops at each checkpoint. There is no turtle here — everything runs against the two packages you build, inside the workspace from Week 2. The freeze on slides 20 to 24 is caused on purpose. Do not fix it early.

SECTION 1

Custom Interface Packages

4Live

Two Tools: ament and colcon

A workspace is a building site. ament is the standard each package is built to. colcon is the foreman: it reads the plans, decides who works first, and never picks up a tool itself. Two commands make this real before anyone has to choose a build type.

  1. $ros2 pkg list | wc -l

    T2 What it does: counts the packages installed on this computer. wc -l counts lines.

    You will see — a number near this
    579
  2. $ros2 pkg prefix turtlesim

    What it does: prints the folder where one package was installed.

    You will see
    /opt/ros/jazzy
The keyline

colcon decides when each package is built. ament decides how. Nearly 600 packages, each built by its own ament build type, all found through one install folder. That is the scale colcon exists for.

5Live

Package Layout for Custom Interfaces

Everyone types these three lines. Two packages, two different build types, and the reason for the difference is on the slide.

  1. $cd ~/ee414_ws/src

    T2 What it does: moves into the src folder of the workspace you made in Week 2. New packages always go here.

  2. $ros2 pkg create ee414_w03_interfaces --build-type ament_cmake

    What it does: creates the package that will hold your message and service definitions. It uses ament_cmake because turning a .msg file into a class you can import is a CMake job.

  3. $ros2 pkg create ee414_w03_nodes --build-type ament_python --dependencies rclpy std_msgs

    What it does: creates the package that will hold your Python nodes, the same way as last week. --dependencies writes the two names into package.xml for you.

Two build types

ament_cmake for the definitions. ament_python for the nodes. This is the first week you have to choose, which is why slide 4 exists.

6Talk

Package Creation Output

Ask them to read the build type and dependencies lines back to you before moving on. That is the whole check, and it catches the mistake on the next slide before it costs anyone twenty minutes.

7Break it

A Common pkg create Error

Type it wrongly, on purpose, in front of them.

  1. $ros2 pkg create --build-type ament_python --dependencies rclpy std_msgs ee414_w03_nodes

    T2 What it does: nothing. It fails. The only change from slide 5 is that the package name is now at the end.

    It fails with
    error: the following arguments are required: package_name
Why

--dependencies accepts a list, so it swallows ee414_w03_nodes as a third dependency. Then nothing is left to be the package name, and the error complains about package_name — the one thing the student did type.

The rule

Package name first, options after. Two minutes here saves twenty minutes of somebody's lab hour.

8Live

Writing the Interface Definitions

  1. $cd ~/ee414_ws/src/ee414_w03_interfaces

    T2 What it does: moves into the interfaces package you just created.

  2. $mkdir msg srv

    What it does: creates the two folders. The names must be exactly msg and srv — the generator looks for those names.

Then write

msg/WheelState.msg — a header, two float64, one bool. srv/ResetOdom.srv — one field, then ---, then two fields. File names use CamelCase. Field names use snake_case. The generator enforces both.

9Talk

Build Configuration in CMakeLists.txt

Tell them to copy these lines from the lab sheet. Nobody remembers rosidl_generate_interfaces, including you. Only one line is worth explaining: DEPENDENCIES std_msgs. It is needed because WheelState contains a Header, and leaving it out fails with an error about an unknown type.

10Live

Building and Verifying the Package

  1. $cd ~/ee414_ws

    T2 What it does: moves to the top of the workspace. Always build from here, never from inside a package.

  2. $colcon build --symlink-install

    What it does: builds every package in the workspace. --symlink-install links your Python files instead of copying them, so small edits do not need a rebuild.

    You will see
    Starting >>> ee414_w03_interfaces
Finished <<< ee414_w03_interfaces [6.10s]
Starting >>> ee414_w03_nodes
Finished <<< ee414_w03_nodes [1.23s]

Summary: 2 packages finished [7.48s]
  3. $source install/setup.bash

    What it does: tells this terminal where the new packages are. Without this line, the next command cannot find your message. Every new terminal needs it again.

Watch the order

ee414_w03_interfaces must finish before ee414_w03_nodes starts. colcon works this out from package.xml. If it builds them the other way round, a dependency line is missing.

If it fails

No module named 'em' means Anaconda is active. Run conda deactivate, then build again. Expect two or three students to hit this. Say it out loud before they do.

11Live

Generated Interfaces: ros2 interface show

  1. $ros2 interface show ee414_w03_interfaces/msg/WheelState

    T2 What it does: asks ROS 2 to print your message. The same command as slide 12 of Deck A, now pointed at something you wrote.

    You will see
    std_msgs/Header  header
	builtin_interfaces/Time stamp
		int32 sec
		uint32 nanosec
	string frame_id
float64          left_rad_s
float64          right_rad_s
bool             estopped
  2. $ros2 interface show ee414_w03_interfaces/srv/ResetOdom

    What it does: prints your service. One separator, as expected.

    You will see
    bool zero_heading
---
bool success
string message
Notice

Their .msg file had four lines. This output has eight. Header was opened up, because show follows every nested type down to plain numbers and text.

12Talk

Checkpoint 1

Stop here. Everyone's package builds, and interface show prints their own type. The question on the slide — why do we run source install/setup.bash after every build? — separates the students who will debug their own workspace from the ones who will ask you to.

SECTION 2

Publishing on a Topic

14Live

Using a Custom Message in a Node

  1. $ros2 run ee414_w03_nodes wheel_publisher

    T4 What it does: starts the node that sends WheelState messages. Leave it running for the rest of the session.

The one line that matters

from ee414_w03_interfaces.msg import WheelState. The package they built two slides ago is now importable like any other Python module. That is what the build was for.

15Live

Verifying the Custom Message on the Wire

  1. $ros2 topic echo /wheel_state --once

    T2 What it does: reads one message off the channel and prints it.

    You will see — your stamp will differ
    header:
  stamp:
    sec: 1788613547
    nanosec: 75208977
  frame_id: base_link
left_rad_s: 2.4
right_rad_s: 2.4
estopped: false
---
Say this

ros2 topic echo has never heard of WheelState. It reads the definition out of your package at runtime and prints your message correctly. Your type is now a first-class ROS 2 type.

SECTION 3

Service Server and Client

17Live

The Service Server

  1. $ros2 run ee414_w03_nodes odom_node

    T4 What it does: starts the node that offers the /reset_odom service. Open a second tab for this — the wheel publisher must keep running.

18Live

Testing the Service from the Command Line

  1. $ros2 service list | grep reset

    T2 What it does: finds your service in the list. grep reset keeps only the lines containing that word.

    You will see
    /reset_odom
  2. $ros2 service call /reset_odom ee414_w03_interfaces/srv/ResetOdom "{zero_heading: true}"

    What it does: calls your service and waits for the reply. Same three parts as Deck A slide 20: name, type, request.

    You will see
    requester: making request: ee414_w03_interfaces.srv.ResetOdom_Request(zero_heading=True)

response:
ee414_w03_interfaces.srv.ResetOdom_Response(success=True, message='odometry zeroed')
Say this

No client code has been written yet. The terminal is the client. You can always test a service before you write anything that calls it.

SECTION 4

Executor Deadlock

20Break it

Attempt 1: Blocking on the Future

The loud failure. One node with three behaviours, chosen by a mode parameter — so the same program can fail in two different ways, and then work.

  1. $ros2 run ee414_w03_nodes reset_client --ros-args -p mode:=spin

    T2 What it does: runs the client in the first wrong way. --ros-args -p name:=value is how you set a parameter when starting a node. This is meant to fail.

    It fails with
      File "/opt/ros/jazzy/lib/python3.12/site-packages/rclpy/executors.py", line 370, in spin_until_future_complete
    self._enter_spin()
  File "/opt/ros/jazzy/lib/python3.12/site-packages/rclpy/executors.py", line 222, in _enter_spin
    raise RuntimeError('Executor is already spinning')
RuntimeError: Executor is already spinning
[ros2run]: Process exited with failure 1
Notice

The error is loud, immediate, and it names the problem. This is the lucky failure. The next one is worse.

21Break it

Attempt 2: Synchronous call()

This is the one that matters. Run it, then stop talking. Let the silence last a full fifteen seconds. The room becoming uncomfortable is the lesson.

  1. $ros2 run ee414_w03_nodes reset_client --ros-args -p mode:=hang

    T2 What it does: runs the client in the second wrong way. It prints two lines and then freezes forever. Press Ctrl-C when you are ready.

    It prints, then stops
    [INFO] [1788613552.048389485] [reset_client]: mode=hang - subscribed to /wheel_state
[INFO] [1788613552.513192689] [reset_client]: callback: calling the service, waiting for the reply ...

(nothing else, for as long as you leave it)
Ask first

Is it broken, or is it just slow? They cannot tell from the terminal — and neither can you. No error, no exit code, no clue. That is why this failure is worse than the first one.

22Talk

The Cause of the Deadlock

There is one thread, and it runs callbacks one at a time. The message callback is holding that thread while it waits for a reply. But the reply can only be delivered by that same thread. So it waits forever. Draw it on the board if the picture on the slide does not land.

23Talk

The Fix: Callback-Based Completion

Use call_async, then add_done_callback. Return from the callback straight away and let the executor deliver the reply when it arrives. One sentence to remember: never wait inside a callback.

24Live

The Corrected Client in Operation

  1. $ros2 run ee414_w03_nodes reset_client --ros-args -p mode:=fix

    T2 What it does: runs the same program the correct way. Press Ctrl-C when the point is made.

    You will see, once per message
    [INFO] [1788613567.725090059] [reset_client]: reply: odometry zeroed
[INFO] [1788613568.013522769] [reset_client]: reply: odometry zeroed
[INFO] [1788613568.076309120] [reset_client]: reply: odometry zeroed
[INFO] [1788613568.225436732] [reset_client]: reply: odometry zeroed
Notice

Same node, same service, one changed line. The output goes from nothing at all to one reply per message, forever.

SECTION 5

Parameters

26Live

Declaring and Reading Parameters

  1. $ros2 run ee414_w03_nodes driver

    T4 What it does: starts a node that prints its two settings every 2 seconds. Leave it running and keep it visible.

    You will see, every 2 seconds
    max_speed=0.22 frame_id=base_link
The important detail

The values are read inside the timer callback, not stored once in __init__. That is the only reason the next slide works.

27Live

Modifying a Parameter at Runtime

Keep T4 on screen. The printed line changes while the node keeps running.

  1. $ros2 param list /driver

    T2 What it does: lists the settings of your own node, the same way as turtlesim's.

  2. $ros2 param get /driver max_speed

    What it does: reads the current speed limit.

    You will see
    Double value is: 0.22
  3. $ros2 param set /driver max_speed 0.05

    What it does: lowers the limit while the node runs. Watch T4.

    You will see
    Set parameter successful
  4. $ros2 param get /driver max_speed

    What it does: reads it back, to prove the change was kept.

    You will see
    Double value is: 0.05
Checkpoint 5

Everyone has now changed how a running program behaves, from the terminal, without restarting it. That is tuning. It is how they will find controller gains in Week 5 and safety distances in Week 11.

28Live

Persisting Parameter Values

A value set from the terminal disappears when the node restarts. Prove it before you show the launch file.

  1. T4 First: press Ctrl-C to stop the driver.

  2. $ros2 run ee414_w03_nodes driver

    What it does: starts it again. The value you set is gone.

    You will see — back to the default
    max_speed=0.22 frame_id=base_link
  3. $ros2 param dump /driver

    T2 What it does: prints all current values as YAML. A fast way to save what you tuned before you type it into the launch file.

The workflow

Tune with param set until it behaves. Then write the value you found into the launch file. Students who skip the second step spend demo day wondering why the robot is worse than it was yesterday.

SECTION 6

Action Clients

30Live

Observing an Action from the Command Line

  1. $ros2 run action_tutorials_py fibonacci_action_server

    T4 What it does: starts a ready-made action server that computes Fibonacci numbers slowly, on purpose. Open a third tab. It comes with ROS 2; you do not have to write it.

  2. $ros2 action send_goal /fibonacci action_tutorials_interfaces/action/Fibonacci "{order: 3}" --feedback

    T2 What it does: asks for the first 3 numbers and shows the progress. Watch the sequence grow by one number per update.

    Expected output — goal, feedback, result
    Waiting for an action server to become available...
Sending goal:
     order: 3

Goal accepted with ID: e372ae4b0cc046fcb05356ca49546688

Feedback:
    partial_sequence:
- 0
- 1
- 1

Feedback:
    partial_sequence:
- 0
- 1
- 1
- 2

Result:
    sequence:
- 0
- 1
- 1
- 2

Goal finished with status: SUCCEEDED
  3. $ros2 action send_goal /fibonacci action_tutorials_interfaces/action/Fibonacci "{order: 3}"

    What it does: the same goal with no --feedback. You wait in silence, then get the answer. The difference between these two runs is the entire reason actions exist.

Notice

The goal ID is different every run. The sequence is not. The partial sequence is the same list, growing — that is what feedback means.

31Talk

The Action Client

Three callbacks — goal accepted, feedback, result — and the same rule as the service client: return immediately and let the executor call you back. The freeze they caused twenty minutes ago is why this shape is not optional.

32Talk

Summary of Capabilities

Read the list back as things they did, not as topics that were covered. They defined a type, generated it, published it, served it, froze it, fixed it and tuned it — in ninety minutes.

Both packages build. interface show prints their own type. The client replies once per message. Week 4 is differential-drive kinematics, where /cmd_vel stops being a demo and becomes mathematics.

Which of these belong on the slides

Deck A shows output on thirteen slides, but it never tells a student what to type. The screenshots were made by a script, so the command exists — it just lives in shoot_w03.py and not on the slide. These six are worth printing under the picture, so the class can follow on their own machines:

  • Slide 7 — ros2 node info /turtlesim. The most useful command in the deck, and right now it is only readable in the prompt line of the screenshot.
  • Slide 12 — both interface show commands, so the class can count the separators themselves instead of being told the answer.
  • Slide 20 — the service call /spawn line. It is long, and students will mistype it from a picture.
  • Slide 25 — action send_goal … --feedback, with the warning to keep theta small.
  • Slide 29 — param get and the three param set lines.
  • Slide 33 — topic hz and topic info --verbose.

Deck B needs none of this. Its typed boxes already carry every command, each one followed by a picture of the result. That is the lab pattern, and it is working.
